Using these links will ensure access to this page indefinitely. # From Coverage to Pairwise-Overlap: Lottery Number Selection under Budget Constraints. 52 Pages Posted: 12 Apr 2024 Last revised: 17 Jun 2025. See all articles by Changchun Liu. ## Changchun Liu. Xi'an Jiaotong University (XJTU) - School of Management. ## Ju Liu. NUS Research Institute (Chong Qing), National University of Singapore. ## Chung-Piaw Teo. NUS Business School - Department of Decision Sciences. Lottery number selection has traditionally been guided by covering design principles: choose the smallest number of tickets needed to ensure that every pair, triple, or higher-order subset of numbers appears somewhere in the ticket set. This classical approach assumes that greater combinatorial coverage leads to higher chances of winning. But under realistic budget constraints---where players can only afford a limited number of tickets---we find that this intuition breaks down. We show that maximizing coverage can paradoxically reduce the chances of winning more lottery  prizes, due to excessive overlap across tickets. The best strategy is not to eliminate overlap, but to structure it—distributing it evenly to balance redundancy and diversity. That this structure arises without explicitly favoring coverage or overlap highlights a deeper universality—robust design under uncertainty favors well-distributed, structured redundancy. We formalize this concept and develop efficient algorithms to construct such ticket sets, drawing inspiration from combinatorial design theory and implementing a randomized ``nibble'' heuristic that incrementally builds high-performing portfolios. Lotteries are widely played, often by individuals with limited means, yet most players lack access to effective strategies. Instead of relying on myth or luck, players can make more informed choices by using designs that balance diversity and redundancy. I have implemented a set of "or" constraints in my ILP using binary decision variables (as in this method). It works fine for smaller problems, but when I try to increase the number of variables it gets very slow very fast, such that it is not feasible for the size of problem I need to solve. Without the “or” constraint, the solution is found in a matter of seconds, even for a problem twice the size that I need, so it’s not just a matter of the number of variables (because the decision variables make the simplex no longer convex). All my variables are binary, I am using a GLPK solver from R (Rglpk), running on a professional-grade laptop. I can successfully solve the problem for $1,000$ variables in a couple seconds, while $10,000$ takes a couple hours. My variables are the entries of a binary matching matrix $B$, weighted by a similarity matrix $S$, the constraints are just row sums and column sums:. ## 3 Answers 3. Answers to the linked question mention both big-M constraints and semicontinuous variables. GLPK is not the best performing MILP solver. Instead, you could give one of the leading commercial MILP solvers a try (e.g. Gurobi). Those solvers should be faster out of the box. You can quickly evaluate different solvers with your model by writing it out as `.MPS` file. Every MILP solver I know of can read these files. Some solvers, like Gurobi, have special APIs to formulate OR constraints and indicator constraints. By using these APIs you can sidestep finding a suitable Big-M yourself and let the solver find appropriate values (which may even tightened during the solving process). Still, a million variables is probably challenging for these solvers as well. ## Your Answer. Thanks for contributing an answer to Operations Research Stack Exchange!
